access.reach.measured_on: decided: a screw, then a hex key behind it; not measured
access.reach.description: length of the straight path checked in front of every opening and screw head

access.tool_clearance.measured_on: decided: a 5.5 mm head got a 6.5 mm path
access.tool_clearance.description: the tool path in front of a screw head is wider than the head by this much

access.seal_gap.description: an obstacle nearer than this to a mouth seals it

access.min_blocked_share.measured_on: decided: below it a hit is probe noise; the older check used a blocked volume of 0.3 mm3
access.min_blocked_share.description: share of the path section an obstacle must cover to count

access.cap_max.measured_on: decided after a hole was closed by a 0.84 mm cap and screws were blocked by a 1.5 mm wall
access.cap_max.description: plastic up to this thick between a blind hole end and what continues on the same axis is a closed hole

access.key_long_arm.measured_on: decided: the long arm of a common small L key; measure your own
access.key_long_arm.description: radius the long arm of the L key sweeps round a screw

access.key_short_arm.measured_on: the L key of the owner of one project
access.key_short_arm.description: short arm of the L key: how high the key stands over a head

access.free_height_over_head.measured_on: decided for a key with a 20 mm short arm; not measured
access.free_height_over_head.description: free height over a screw head that lets the key go in and turn

access.key_side_clearance.description: room beside the long arm of the key for the hand

access.key_swing_deg.measured_on: decided: the half-disc of the written rule; a hex key seats again every 60 degrees, so a project may lower it by owner decision
access.key_swing_deg.description: free sector the long arm of the key needs round a screw

access.overlay_pattern.measured_on: a decision of the owner of one project, never a measurement: which bodies are no part of the build. The default matches nothing
access.overlay_pattern.description: a body whose name matches is an overlay (an old version or a scan laid over the model): it covers and seals nothing

rules.title: What an opening is for stays reachable
rules.statement: What must be free in front of an opening depends on what the opening is for. A screw hole: the key side, a straight path of the hole's own section for {access.reach}; of a straight through hole with no screw ref the side that is better off counts, and a hole that holds a screw ref is judged at the head of that screw, on the part the head sits on (a screw is known by its shape first, so a head body and a shank body under any name are one screw). A bearing seat: the side the bearing goes in from, for the width of the bearing, free of the part itself. A slot or window with nothing in it: like a key side. A hole of no table is asked about once (what is it for), an insert pocket has its own rule. Holes on one axis that follow each other within {access.cap_max} are one bore, judged at its outer ends. What sits in an opening by design does not cover it: the fastener and the mating hole on its axis, the bearing in its seat, a bought part or a fastener that reaches into a slot or window (a lock screw in its slot, a motor in its window; a mesh or a printed neighbour inside it is judged like a cover; the rim of the part itself within {access.seal_gap} of such a mouth is no cover either). The path is tested against every body in reach, hidden ones too. The part itself in the path is a finding. Other solid bodies in the paths of a part are ONE row and one question for the part: every covering part nearest first, with its distance and the openings it stands in front of; free only if each is mounted later and comes off first. A body inside a bought or linked assembly is named with the assembly it belongs to. A mesh has no exact shape: it is never a finding, the check stays open until the mesh is a solid body or the owner names it an overlay (the parameter access.overlay_pattern). A hit under {access.min_blocked_share} of the section is noise.
rules.why: The class the owner names: a hole closed by another part. A ledge of the same part covered two motor screws and passed every hole, wall and sliver check. A mount made its neighbour impossible to screw in. The check that existed saw only screws that had ref bodies, and as obstacles only visible printed solids: a motor, a bearing, a pulley, another screw's head, a mesh-only part or a hidden component could not block anything.
fix_order: The part itself in the path: cut it back to the full section of the opening, over the whole length.
Another part in the path that is mounted later and comes off first: answer the assembly-order question and write the order into the build notes.
Another part that is there first: cut it back, move it, or move the opening together with what mates with it.
A mesh in the path: make it a solid body. When it is no part of the build, ask the owner to name it in the overlay pattern.
An opening that lost its function: remove it. A reserve insert under another part is removed or named unusable.
rules.note: First run on a real assembly: a free path of the full reach in front of both ends of every hole gave well over a hundred findings on a handful of parts, nearly all of them what sits in the opening by design (the bearing and its clamp washers, the plate a screw bolts to, the motor a hole screws into) or an old mesh overlay. The rule now asks per kind of opening. Not judged by it: what stands in front of a bearing seat other than the part itself (bearings.insertion_path, not asked yet), and holes of no table (census.unknown_hole asks). Facts from a probe that knew screws by name only: a screw hole with a bought body on its axis is NOT_RUN until the facts are collected again. A blind thread pilot shallower than the least thread engagement of its size (a phasing marker, a spigot socket) holds no screw and needs no key path. A blind slot or window with nothing measured inside it (a lightening pocket between ribs) needs no key path either: one INFO row counts them.

rules.title: Every screw can be put in and turned
rules.statement: In front of every screw head a straight path is free for {access.reach}, for the screw and the key behind it. The part itself must not stand in the section of the head, nor farther out than {access.seal_gap} anywhere in the path as wide as the head plus {access.tool_clearance}: not even a thin ledge over the edge of a head seat. The part itself in the ring of the tool clearance right at the top of the head is the wall of the recess the head sits in, not a ledge. Other solid bodies in the paths of a part are ONE row and one question for the part, whatever they are: every covering part nearest first, with its distance and the heads it covers; free only if each is fitted later and comes off first, with its removal order named. A body is a cover of a head only within {assembly.cover_reach} of the head top: the bodies farther out are said in one row, not asked, because an L key reaches the head under them (access.key_swing judges its swing). A body inside a bought or linked assembly is named with the assembly it belongs to. A mesh in the path leaves the check open. Every fastener exists as a ref body before this check runs; a screw that is only a hole is tested as a hole. A hit under {access.min_blocked_share} of the section is noise; a body the owner named an overlay (access.overlay_pattern) is not counted.
rules.why: A printed ledge over the edge of a head seat passed every hole, wall and sliver check on the biggest part of a build: two screws could not go in. Later two heads sat under parts fitted afterwards, by design, and were named nowhere but in a design log.
fix_order: Cut the ledge back to the head seat plus the tool clearance.
Move the screw, or let it come in from the free side.
A head under a part fitted later: answer the assembly-order question with the removal order.
A screw that is serviced on the finished machine: add a service hole through the cover.
rules.note: The asked row keeps its id, and an answer or a waiver holds, while the same parts stand in front of the same heads, however far out. It is asked again, with the whole list, when a covering part joins or leaves, and when one comes to stand in front of another head or leaves one: a cover is named by its component, which can hold many bodies, and an answer never covers a part, or a place of a part, it did not name. A mesh body keeps a row of its own.

rules.title: No mouth is sealed
rules.statement: No pocket or hole is closed over its whole section, at every end it has, by a body nearer than {access.seal_gap}, unless that body is the fastener or the mating hole that belongs there. A blind pocket has one end. A through hole that lies against a plate at one end still takes its pin or insert from the other; holes on one axis within {access.cap_max} of each other are one bore. A plain screw clearance hole needs both ends, one for the key and one for the thread behind it: one sealed end closes it. A sealed hole takes no screw, insert, pin or cable, whatever the assembly order. A body the owner named an overlay (access.overlay_pattern) seals nothing.
rules.why: A sealed insert pocket existed on a lug, and insert mouths sat hidden under a collar wall: nothing could ever be fitted into them.
fix_order: Open the mouth: cut the covering body over the full section.
Move the pocket to a free face.
Remove the pocket if it lost its function.

rules.title: A hole is open end to end
rules.statement: A hole does not end in a skin of material up to {access.cap_max} thick where its stack, a coaxial hole or a screw shank says it goes on. After any join, fill, fillet or growth of the body every hole and pocket of the zone is checked again along its axis. Solids first, cuts last. A fillet must not eat a functional feature. One exception is asked, never passed in silence: a bridge layer, a skin of at most {overhang.bridge_step} between a counterbore that faces the bed and its narrower hole, which is opened after the print. A counterbore that does not face the bed (flatter than {overhang.max_angle}) needs none: there the skin is a finding.
rules.why: A join after a cut half-filled two screw holes. Body growth left a 0.84 mm cap in a screw hole of a printed part: it was drilled by hand. Clamp screws were blocked by a 1.5 mm wall in front of their inserts. A 0.2 mm fill skin closed another hole. Each was found in the slicer or on the bench: the check that existed looked only at insert pockets.
fix_order: Cut the hole through all, or 1 mm past the far face; never to a typed depth.
Cut holes after the last join or fill of the zone.
Run the gate again after every join, fill or fillet: the hole census of the part must not lose a hole or an open end.
rules.note: Two blind holes that meet at one cap are one finding, at the wider hole. A cap that may be a bridge layer is asked through access.bridge_layer. A blind thread pilot shallower than the least thread engagement of its size is closed on purpose: no row.

rules.title: A bridge layer is meant, and opened after the print
rules.statement: A one-layer skin between a counterbore that faces the bed and its hole is a print aid: the ring round the hole cannot print in the air. It is allowed when it is meant, and the build notes say that the hole is pushed or drilled through after the print. A skin of the same thickness that a join or a fill left behind is a closed hole.
rules.why: A 0.2 mm fill skin closed a hole and was found in the slicer. A bridge layer of 0.3 mm under a head seat looks the same in the model: only the designer knows which one it is.
fix_order: A leftover skin: cut the hole through all, after the last join or fill of the zone.
A bridge layer: write into the build notes which holes are opened after the print, and with what.

attest.question: Hole {feature} ends in a skin one bridge step thick, with hole {by} behind it. Is it a bridge layer that is opened after the print?
labels: a bridge layer under a counterbore that faces the bed: it is opened after the print, and the build notes say so

rules.note: Asked through the finding of access.hole_closed. When it is a leftover skin no label is true: cut the hole through, and the finding is gone.

rules.title: No hole is closed by supports
rules.statement: No hole, tunnel or slot is closed by supports. A hole whose axis is off the print axis gets a roofed section, or a support blocker in every project it is placed in, or it is sliced and looked at. A mesh swap keeps a blocker where it was: after a hole moves, its blocker is checked again.
rules.why: Three clamp holes were closed by supports and drilled out. A tunnel for a tension screw came out full of supports twice. A cable holder was unusable with support stuck in its tie tunnel.
fix_order: Turn the part so the hole axis is the print axis.
Give the hole a roof that prints without support.
Put a support blocker over the hole in every project that holds the part, and check it again after the hole moves.

attest.question: For every hole, tunnel and slot of this part that is off the print axis: what keeps supports out of it?
labels: every such hole has a roof that prints without support
every hole of this part is along the print axis
looked at in the sliced plate: no support inside any hole
off-axis holes without a roof: listed in the report; a blocker or a look at the sliced plate is owed in every project it is placed in

rules.note: Asked at export, once per changed part. At that moment a new geometry is in no .3mf project yet, and in enforce mode it gets into one only with its stamp. So answer from the model: the roof label or the axis label when it is true. Take the "looked at in the sliced plate" label only when this geometry was sliced (a part that is exported again, or observe mode). Otherwise take the last label: the report lists it for the owner, and the blocker or the look at the slice is done after the part is placed, before the print. No probe reads the support blockers of the .3mf or the support paths of a slice yet: the answer is the check.

rules.title: The key can turn at every screw
rules.statement: A screw is reachable only if the key can also turn. Over each head {access.free_height_over_head} is free for a key with a {access.key_short_arm} short arm, or a straight line for a long key exists. The long arm ({access.key_long_arm}) sweeps at least {access.key_swing_deg} free of every part fitted before it, with {access.key_side_clearance} beside the arm.
rules.why: Corner gussets blocked 8 of 10 screws of a mount for the L key, although every straight path was free. Three gusset versions were designed, one was exported to plates, and the base was redesigned from scratch.
fix_order: Move the gusset, rib or wall out of the swing of the key.
Move the screw to where the key can turn.
Open a straight line for a long key through the part that stands in the way.
rules.note: Measured by fusion_openings over every screw head seated on the part: the long arm of an L key, access.key_short_arm above the head, as a path of radius access.key_side_clearance / 2 in 12 directions round the axis. A head the key cannot swing over but a straight key reaches from above is an INFO row (the build notes name the key); a head neither reaches fails. Bodies fitted after the part are not told apart from those fitted before.

rules.title: A head under a later part is a named exception
rules.statement: A screw head covered by a part fitted later is an exception with a name and a removal order: which part comes off first, and with which key. It is answered through the assembly-order question of the finding, never by leaving the screw ref out of the model. Where a standard length gives a flush head, prefer it.
rules.why: Two heads sat under later parts by design: one in a well under a bracket foot, one under an end plate in a trough 3.6 mm high. Both were named only in a design log.
fix_order: Write the removal order into the build notes when the question is answered.
Look for a shared screw set that leaves the head on the outer part.

rules.title: What is adjusted later has a tool path on the finished machine
rules.statement: Anything adjusted or replaced after assembly (belt tension, preload, set screws, a switch) has a tool path on the finished machine. The key type and its reach are stated. A covered screw gets a service hole or a recorded removal order.
rules.why: A joint could not be assembled as drawn. The access to an adjustment under a link was never checked.
fix_order: List what is adjusted on the finished machine and check the path of each with all parts mounted.

rules.title: Every fastener is a ref body before access is checked
rules.statement: Every fastener exists as a ref body before the access check runs. A screw that is only a hole is tested with the section of the hole, not with the head and the key: the head path is not proven.
rules.why: A blocked screw was found by the owner on the model: it had no ref body, so the check could not see it.
fix_order: Place the screw refs of a part before its gate run.

rules.title: Every hole has a known purpose
rules.statement: A hole the census cannot classify against the tables is named once: a blind one, or one with a bought body on its axis, through the question what goes in it (fits.pocket_content), every other one here. A short cylinder that is a piece of the same surface as another hole is not asked about. Named here too is a straight hole that is both a clearance hole and the old straight pocket of an insert, a blind hole of clearance size, and a pocket-sized cylinder whose wall is broken open, unless a screw ref lies on its axis. The answer is kept for that hole until the hole changes.
rules.why: Holes nobody could name were leftovers of moved features, or pockets of a wrong size that no check listed.

attest.question: Hole {feature}: what is this hole for?
labels: mates with a bought part (named in the hardware refs)
magnet, peg or sensor pocket (named in the hardware refs)

rules.note: "A screw that is not modelled yet" is no answer any more: hardware.refs_present fails a screw hole with no screw ref.
